How should missing values, duplicate rows, and IQR outliers be handled? 2. What does one row represent after aggregating passengers by class and sex? 3. Why can stratified sampling keep small groups that simple random sampling misses? ::: {.callout-note} ## Implement in `lab02_1.py` first This notebook calls functions from `lab02_1.py`. If that file is missing, it downloads the seaborn Titanic table and saves it there. ::: {#f43cdf0f .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} titanic = load_titanic() type(titanic), titanic.shape ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (pandas.DataFrame, (891, 15)) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#bc9026da .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} titanic.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}

A common replacement is the **mode**, the most frequent value. Together with the mean and the median, it is one of the three standard measures of central tendency. `Series.mode()` returns that most frequent value. If several values are tied, it returns all of them; the code below uses the first. ::: {.callout-important title="Q. Practice"} Implement `fill_missing_with_mode()` in `lab02_1.py`. It should replace missing values in `embarked` with the mode of that column. **Hint:** `Series.mode()` returns the most frequent value, and `Series.fillna()` replaces missing values. ::: {#3cf1cbb8 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} titanic_clean, embarked_mode = fill_missing_with_mode( titanic_clean, column="embarked", ) print( "Mode:", embarked_mode, ) print( "Missing embarked:", titanic_clean["embarked"].isna().sum(), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Mode: S Missing embarked: 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Think"} Why do `age` and `embarked` use different replacement values? `age` is numerical, so the median is defined. `embarked` is categorical, so the median is not defined and we use the mode, the most frequent value. ::: ## 1.3 Duplicate Records Duplicate records can make the same observation count more than once. The Titanic dataset does not include a passenger ID that can be used here to verify true duplicate passengers. To demonstrate duplicate detection, we intentionally copy three rows and append them to a small subset of the data. ::: {#9ff07412 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} titanic_with_duplicates = pd.concat( [ titanic.iloc[:8], titanic.iloc[[1, 3, 5]], ], ignore_index=True, ) titanic_with_duplicates ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}

The first occurrence is marked as `False`, and later identical rows are marked as `True`. ::: {#d30fcb1f .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} duplicate_mask = ( titanic_with_duplicates .duplicated() ) duplicate_mask ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ``` 0 False 1 False 2 False 3 False 4 False 5 False 6 False 7 False 8 True 9 True 10 True dtype: bool ``` ::: ::: The `True` values indicate rows that have already appeared earlier. ::: {#84963550 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} titanic_with_duplicates[ duplicate_mask ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}

It should count duplicate rows and return a DataFrame with them removed. **Hint:** Use `duplicated().sum()` and `drop_duplicates()`. ::: {#f55a6387 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} titanic_without_duplicates, duplicate_count = drop_duplicate_rows( titanic_with_duplicates ) print( "Duplicate rows:", duplicate_count, ) print( "Before:", len(titanic_with_duplicates), ) print( "After:", len(titanic_without_duplicates), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Duplicate rows: 3 Before: 11 After: 8 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## 1.4 Outliers An outlier is an unusually small or large value. A common rule uses the interquartile range (IQR). $$ IQR = Q_3 - Q_1 $$ Values outside the following range are considered potential outliers: $$ [Q_1 - 1.5IQR,\; Q_3 + 1.5IQR] $$ We use Titanic `fare` and first obtain the first and third quartiles. ::: {#48713691 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} fare = ( titanic["fare"] .dropna() ) q1 = fare.quantile(0.25) q3 = fare.quantile(0.75) print( "Q1:", round(q1, 2), ) print( "Q3:", round(q3, 2), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Q1: 7.91 Q3: 31.0 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-important title="Q. Practice"} Implement `iqr_outlier_bounds()` in `lab02_1.py`. It should return the lower and upper fences from `q1` and `q3`. **Hint:** Use `q3 - q1` for the IQR. ::: {#d2e3907e .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} lower, upper = iqr_outlier_bounds( q1, q3, ) outlier_mask = ( (fare > upper) | (fare < lower) ) print( "Lower threshold:", round(lower, 2), ) print( "Upper threshold:", round(upper, 2), ) print( "Potential outliers:", int(outlier_mask.sum()), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Lower threshold: -26.72 Upper threshold: 65.63 Potential outliers: 116 ``` ::: ::: ::: After implementing the function, run the following cell to visualize the potential outliers. ::: {#b92ccfbc .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} plot_fare_outliers( fare, lower, upper, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Potential fare outliers using the IQR rule](lab02-1_files/figure-html/cell-15-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Think"} Does a statistical outlier always mean that the recorded value is wrong? No. The IQR rule only flags values far from the bulk of the data. An unusual fare can still be a real first-class ticket. ::: ## 1.5 Aggregation Aggregation combines two or more objects into a single higher-level object. Objects with the same grouping value are combined into one summary record. For example, we can group passengers by `pclass` and summarize `survived` and `fare`. ::: {#64a11c52 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} class_summary = ( titanic .groupby("pclass") .agg({ "survived": "mean", "fare": "median", }) .reset_index() ) class_summary ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ```{=html}
pclass survived fare

2 3 0.242363 8.0500
``` ::: ::: Each row now represents one passenger class rather than one passenger. ::: {.callout-important title="Q. Practice"} Implement `summarize_by_class_and_sex()` in `lab02_1.py`. Group the passengers by `pclass` and `sex`. For each group, compute the mean of `survived` and the median of `fare`. **Hint:** Use `groupby(["pclass", "sex"])` followed by `agg({...})`. ::: {#4b329944 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} group_summary = summarize_by_class_and_sex( titanic ) group_summary ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ```{=html}

After aggregation, one row is one group, with summary values such as a mean survival rate or a median fare. ::: ## 1.6 Random and Stratified Sampling Simple random sampling gives each object an equal chance to be selected from the full dataset.
